Terms.noCalibrationTitle: Not a Replacement for Hardware Colorimeters
Terms.noCalibrationText: Browser-based software cannot replace physical spectrophotometers, hardware colorimeters (such as Calibrite or Datacolor Spyder), or optical oscilloscopes. Monitor Tester does not generate ICC color profiles, read physical photometric nits, or certify absolute color accuracy (Delta-E).
Terms.disclaimerText: Monitor Tester is provided on an 'AS IS' and 'AS AVAILABLE' basis without warranties of any kind, whether express or implied. While we strive for precision, test results may vary based on operating system display scaling, GPU driver configurations, browser hardware acceleration, and ambient lighting conditions.
Terms.manufacturerText: Display manufacturers enforce their own specific warranty terms regarding pixel defects (such as ISO 9241-307 Class 1 or Class 2 standards, which often define minimum thresholds of stuck or dead subpixels before an RMA is authorized). Identifying a defect on Monitor Tester does not automatically guarantee warranty replacement by your device manufacturer.

Home.aboutP1: Screen Tester is a free online tool for checking your screen, monitor, or display directly in your web browser. It provides visual tests for common display issues such as dead pixels, colors, brightness, contrast, refresh rate, and screen ghosting.
Home.aboutP2: The tool is useful for checking new or used monitors, laptop displays, gaming screens, and other displays without installing additional software. The tests provide visual inspection patterns and should be treated as a practical reference rather than laboratory-grade hardware measurements.
Home.aboutLimitationsDesc: All tests provide visual diagnostic patterns for human inspection under controlled viewing conditions. Screen Tester does not replace optical hardware sensors (such as spectrophotometers, colorimeters, or photodiode oscilloscopes) and does not modify operating-system color profiles. For optimal results, clean your screen, inspect in fullscreen mode (F11), and verify display scaling is set to 100%.

dead-pixel-test.metaDescription: Free online dead pixel test for monitors and screens. Inspect full-screen solid RGB, black, and white backgrounds to detect dead pixels and stuck subpixels.
dead-pixel-test.title: Dead Pixel Test
dead-pixel-test.description_p1: A dead pixel test helps you quickly find defective, dark, or stuck subpixels on your monitor or laptop display. This test displays full-screen pure colors to make any defective pixel immediately visible.
instructions: WHAT TO CHECK: Ensure your screen is clean before starting. Dust can look like dead pixels.
HOW TO USE: Click or use Space / → to cycle through the test colors.

WHAT YOU MAY NOTICE: Carefully scan the entire screen for tiny dots that don't match the background color. A black dot on a white background is typically a dead pixel. A bright dot on a black background is typically a stuck pixel.

color-test.metaDescription: Test your display colors and visual calibration online. Inspect RGB color purity, color balance, and panel uniformity across full-screen color fields.
color-test.title: Color Test & Visual Calibration
color-test.description_p1: Run an online color test to evaluate RGB color reproduction and visual calibration balance across your display. Cycle through primary and secondary full-screen color fields to spot tint shifts, color banding, and uniformity variations.
instructions: WHAT TO CHECK: Cycle through the colors using Space or →.
HOW TO USE: Look for uneven saturation across the screen.
WHAT YOU MAY NOTICE: Check the grayscale patterns for any unwanted color tints (e.g., the gray looking slightly pink or blue). Ensure that primary colors look vibrant and accurate without bleeding.
ABOUT THIS TEST: Provides reference patterns for visual inspection. It does not measure physical panel color accuracy (Delta E).

brightness-test.metaDescription: Calibrate monitor brightness and black level without crushing shadow details. Features PLUGE reference bars, 1% shadow ramps, and peak white windows.
brightness-test.title: Brightness & Black Level Test
brightness-test.description_p1: This test calibrates your monitor's brightness (black level offset) and evaluates luminance capability. Setting brightness properly ensures deep, inky blacks without crushing shadow details into pure black or washing out dark scenes.
instructions: WHAT TO CHECK (PLUGE BARS): On the default PLUGE pattern, inspect the vertical bars against the black background. Bar 0% is true reference black. Adjust your monitor's physical Brightness setting until Bar +2% (RGB 5) is just barely discernible from black.

BLACK CRUSH WARNING: If you cannot distinguish Bar +1% or Bar +2% from the background, your brightness is set too low (shadow details are crushed into pure black). If the black background looks glowing or gray, your brightness is set too high (washed-out black level).
1% SHADOW RAMP: Switch to the 1% Shadow Ramp mode to check fine near-black steps (0% to 10%) and identify your display's exact black clipping threshold.

PEAK LUMINANCE & ABL: Switch to Peak & ABL Windows to test sustained full-screen white (100%) versus a 10% peak window. Notice whether your OLED, mini-LED, or laptop display dims due to Automatic Brightness Limiting (ABL).

contrast-test.metaDescription: Evaluate your monitor's contrast ratio and white level separation. Ensure bright highlights remain clear without clipping whites into flat blocks.
contrast-test.title: Contrast Calibration Test
contrast-test.description_p1: This test helps you configure your monitor's contrast ratio and gamma response by displaying a 25-step gradient grid from 0% pure black to 100% pure white.
contrast-test.inst1: Inspect the grid blocks to ensure adjacent contrast steps are visually distinct.
contrast-test.inst2: Adjust your monitor's Contrast setting so that blocks 92% and 96% do not blend into 100% white.
contrast-test.inst3: Toggle numerical percentages or switch between brightness and contrast modes using the controls below.

ghosting-test.metaDescription: Free monitor ghosting test to measure pixel response time and motion blur. Inspect moving visual patterns to detect ghosting trails and overdrive coronas.
ghosting-test.title: Ghosting Test
ghosting-test.description_p1: This monitor ghosting test evaluates pixel response times and motion clarity. By watching moving patterns at different speeds, you can easily identify trailing ghosting artifacts or overshoot (coronas) caused by aggressive monitor overdrive settings.
instructions: WHAT TO CHECK: Focus your eyes on the moving blocks. Do not stare statically at the center of the screen.
HOW TO USE: Look for trailing shadows (ghosting) behind the moving blocks.

WHAT YOU MAY NOTICE: If you see a bright/inverted colored trail, this is inverse ghosting (overshoot), usually caused by setting your monitor's overdrive setting too high. Adjust the speed and contrast controls to test different pixel transition scenarios.
ABOUT THIS TEST: This is a visual aid for detecting ghosting. A web browser cannot precisely measure pixel response time (GtG or MPRT) in milliseconds.

refresh-rate-test.metaDescription: Free online refresh rate test to check your monitor's real-time refresh rate (Hz) and frame pacing. Verify 60Hz, 120Hz, 144Hz, 240Hz, or 360Hz display speed.
refresh-rate-test.title: Refresh Rate Test
refresh-rate-test.description_p1: This refresh rate test measures your monitor's active refresh rate (Hz) and frame synchronization directly inside your browser. Verify whether your display is properly running at its advertised 60Hz, 144Hz, 240Hz, or higher refresh rate.
instructions: WHAT TO CHECK: Browsers usually cap rendering at your primary monitor's refresh rate (e.g., 60Hz, 120Hz, 144Hz).
HOW TO USE: Make sure you do not have background video playback running, as some browsers down-clock animations to match video framerates.

WHAT YOU MAY NOTICE: For multi-monitor setups, drag the browser window to the screen you want to test. If the reading is significantly lower than expected, check your OS display settings or GPU control panel to ensure your refresh rate isn't artificially capped.
ABOUT THIS TEST: This test estimates refresh rate based on browser rendering timing (requestAnimationFrame). It is a software estimate, not a direct hardware measurement.

backlight-bleed-test.metaDescription: Detect corner light bleed, cloudy patches, and IPS glow on LCD, LED, and mini-LED displays in a darkened environment.
backlight-bleed-test.title: Backlight Bleed Test
backlight-bleed-test.description_p1: This test renders a pure black screen. It is designed to expose backlight bleed, clouding, or IPS glow that typically affects LCD/LED panels.
instructions: WHAT TO CHECK: This test must be performed in a completely dark room.
HOW TO USE: Set your monitor to its standard or calibrated brightness level (do not force 100% brightness unless that is how you normally use it).

WHAT YOU MAY NOTICE: Look at the corners and edges of the screen. Backlight Bleed appears as distinct patches of white/yellow light leaking from the bezel. IPS Glow shifts and changes intensity as you move your viewing angle.

bright-pixel-test.metaDescription: Identify permanently lit bright pixels and hot subpixels against true black and dark gray backgrounds with color isolation masks.
bright-pixel-test.title: Bright Pixel Test
bright-pixel-test.description_p1: A bright pixel (also called a hot pixel) occurs when a liquid crystal subpixel or OLED emitter is permanently stuck in the on state, emitting light against dark and black backgrounds.
instructions: WHAT TO CHECK: Test in a dimly lit room for maximum visual contrast against the dark background.
HOW TO USE: Press Space or → to cycle between pure black, dark gray, and single-channel RGB isolation masks.
WHAT YOU MAY NOTICE: An illuminated dot on a black screen is a bright or stuck subpixel. Click 'Mark Defect' in the control bar to record its exact coordinates.

stuck-pixel-test.metaDescription: Free online stuck pixel test for monitors and screens. Inspect pure dark fields and primary color masks to isolate and detect stuck RGB subpixels.
stuck-pixel-test.title: Stuck Pixel Test
stuck-pixel-test.description_p1: A stuck pixel test helps you inspect your screen for individual subpixels that remain continuously illuminated with red, green, or blue light. Inspect dark backgrounds and color channels to distinguish stuck subpixels from dead pixels.
instructions: WHAT TO CHECK: Ensure your screen is clean before starting. Dust can look like pixel defects.
HOW TO USE: Press Space or → to cycle between dark fields and primary color masks.
WHAT YOU MAY NOTICE: An illuminated pinpoint of red, green, or blue on a black background is a stuck subpixel. If detected, you can attempt visual cycling using our Stuck Pixel Fixer tool.

uniformity-test.metaDescription: Inspect full-panel brightness uniformity and Dirty Screen Effect (DSE) using 5%, 10%, 20%, 50%, and 100% white reference fields.
uniformity-test.title: Screen Uniformity & DSE Test
uniformity-test.description_p1: This test displays stepped grayscale backgrounds to help identify backlight bleeding, edge darkening (vignetting), and Dirty Screen Effect (DSE).
instructions: WHAT TO CHECK: Check the corners and edges on the 5% and 10% dark grays for clouding or light bleed.
HOW TO USE: On the 20% and 50% grays, look for splotches, bands, or "dirty" smudges across the center of the screen (DSE).
WHAT YOU MAY NOTICE: On the 100% white screen, check if any section of the screen looks warmer (pink/yellow) or cooler (blue) than the rest.
ABOUT THIS TEST: This test provides reference backgrounds for visual inspection. It does not measure physical panel luminance variance.

black-level-test.metaDescription: Check near-black luminance thresholds (0% to 5%) to detect black crush and verify accurate shadow separation.
black-level-test.title: Black Level Test
black-level-test.description_p1: This test helps you configure your monitor's black level (brightness) setting. It displays extremely dark shades near pure black.
black-level-test.inst1: Turn off room lights or reduce glare on the screen.
black-level-test.inst2: Adjust your monitor's 'Brightness' setting until you can barely distinguish block 1 from the pure black background.
black-level-test.inst3: If blocks 1-5 look identical to the background, your blacks are being crushed.

white-level-test.metaDescription: Examine near-white luminance steps (95% to 100%) to ensure bright highlights are not clipped into solid white.
white-level-test.title: White Level Test
white-level-test.description_p1: This test helps you configure your monitor's white level (contrast) setting. It displays extremely bright shades near pure white.
white-level-test.inst1: Adjust your monitor's 'Contrast' setting until you can distinguish block 254 from the pure white background.
white-level-test.inst2: If blocks 250-254 look identical to the background, your whites are clipping.
white-level-test.inst3: Do not set contrast so high that bright details are lost.

grayscale-test.metaDescription: Evaluate grayscale neutrality and color temperature shifts across smooth 256-step linear ramps and stepped bars.
grayscale-test.title: Grayscale Test
grayscale-test.description_p1: This test displays neutral grayscale backgrounds. It helps you check if your monitor suffers from unwanted color tints in its gray rendering.
grayscale-test.inst1: Cycle through the gray levels using Space or right arrow.
grayscale-test.inst2: Look for pink, blue, or green tints in what should be neutral gray.
grayscale-test.inst3: Use your monitor's RGB balance controls to correct any color cast.

saturation-test.metaDescription: Assess color saturation thresholds across Red, Green, Blue, Cyan, Magenta, and Yellow stepped gradients.
saturation-test.title: Saturation Test
saturation-test.description_p1: This test displays a continuous color spectrum and stepped saturation blocks for primary colors.
saturation-test.inst1: Check the smooth spectrum for obvious banding or harsh transitions.
saturation-test.inst2: Look at the individual saturation steps to ensure distinct differences between blocks.
saturation-test.inst3: Adjust your monitor's saturation/vibrancy settings if colors look washed out or overly neon.

gamma-test.metaDescription: Verify display gamma curve tracking against standard Gamma 2.2 and 2.4 reference luminance targets.
gamma-test.title: Gamma Calibration
gamma-test.description_p1: This tool helps you estimate your monitor's physical gamma curve. A gamma of 2.2 is the standard for sRGB and Windows PCs.
gamma-test.inst1: Enter fullscreen and move away from the monitor, or squint your eyes until the top lines blur into a solid gray.
gamma-test.inst2: Compare the blurred top half to the three solid blocks below.
gamma-test.inst3: The block that perfectly matches the brightness of the blurred top half indicates your monitor's approximate gamma.
gamma-test.inst4: ABOUT THIS TEST: This tool relies on visual perception and standard browser color rendering. It is not a replacement for a hardware colorimeter.

motion-blur-test.metaDescription: Analyze motion resolution and persistence blur on fast-paced scenes and moving test objects.
motion-blur-test.title: Motion Blur Test
motion-blur-test.description_p1: Assess how well your monitor handles fast motion without blurring or smearing details.
motion-blur-test.inst1: Track the moving blocks with your eyes.
motion-blur-test.inst2: Look at the small inner square. If the edges blur completely, your monitor has a slow pixel response time.
motion-blur-test.inst3: Adjust speed and contrast to test under different panel overdrive scenarios.

hdr-capability-test.metaDescription: Detect browser HDR support, peak nit luminance capabilities, and wide color gamut reproduction (Display P3 / Rec.2020).
hdr-capability-test.title: HDR Capability Test
hdr-capability-test.description_p1: This tool queries your browser's APIs to determine if High Dynamic Range (HDR) and Wide Color Gamut (P3) are currently enabled and supported by your display chain.
hdr-capability-test.inst2: If it says 'Not Supported' but your monitor is HDR-capable, ensure HDR is turned on in Windows/macOS display settings.
hdr-capability-test.inst3: Ensure you are using a modern browser with hardware acceleration enabled.

display-info.metaDescription: View detected screen resolution, device pixel ratio (DPR), color depth, GPU renderer, and browser capabilities.
display-info.title: Display Information
display-info.description_p1: This data is read directly from your browser's Web APIs. It represents what the browser can detect about your display setup. Note that operating system scaling settings (e.g., Windows UI scaling at 125% or macOS Retina scaling) will affect the "Logical Resolution" reported here.

gradient-test.metaDescription: Identify color banding artifacts and verify smooth 8-bit, 10-bit, or FRC color transitions across linear gradients.
gradient-test.title: Gradient Banding Test
gradient-test.description_p1: Displays a perfectly smooth 24-bit (16.7 million colors) gradient. On lower quality panels or with restricted bit-depth settings, you will see banding (distinct vertical or horizontal lines instead of a smooth transition).
instructions: WHAT TO CHECK: Look closely at the transition from black to the target color.
HOW TO USE: A true 10-bit or high-quality 8-bit+FRC panel will display a buttery smooth transition.
WHAT YOU MAY NOTICE: If you see obvious vertical stripes (stair-stepping), your display is struggling with color depth. Use Space or arrow keys to cycle gradients.

vrr-test.metaDescription: Visually inspect variable refresh rate (VRR), G-Sync, and FreeSync frame pacing under dynamic workloads. Check for judder, stutter, and tearing online.
vrr-test.title: VRR / Adaptive Sync Visual Inspection
vrr-test.description_p1: This test helps you visually inspect variable refresh rate behavior and animation frame pacing under changing frame workloads. Browser animation timing can provide evidence about frame pacing consistency, but cannot prove that a specific VRR hardware mode is engaged.
instructions: SETUP GUIDANCE: 1. Enable VRR / FreeSync / G-Sync Compatible in your monitor's OSD menu. 2. Enable Variable Refresh Rate or G-Sync in Windows/GPU control panel. 3. Enter Fullscreen for optimal frame presentation.
MOTION WORKLOADS: Switch between Low (30 FPS), Medium (60 FPS), High (Max rAF), and Dynamic Sweep workloads to observe frame pacing stability across varied refresh rates.
WHAT TO WATCH FOR: Watch the vertical bars and pendulum. Notice whether the motion remains fluid and tear-free, or exhibits tearing, stutter, judder, or uneven pacing.

hdr-test.metaDescription: Controlled visual HDR inspection pattern to check specular highlight preservation, tone curve rolloff, shadow detail, and wide gamut color rendering.
hdr-test.title: HDR Visual Inspection
hdr-test.description_p1: Provides a controlled visual HDR inspection workflow to evaluate highlight clipping, tone curve rolloff, and near-black separation. Peak luminance in nits requires physical laboratory equipment; this visual test evaluates relative tone reproduction in your browser.
instructions: OS & DISPLAY SETUP: Verify that HDR is toggled ON in Windows Display Settings or macOS System Settings, and that your monitor's HDR picture mode is active.
HIGHLIGHT CLIPPING: Inspect the specular highlight steps (90% to 100%). Look for the point where bright segments blend together or clip into solid white.
SHADOW & WIDE GAMUT: Check near-black blocks (0% to 10%) for shadow crush, and compare the standard SDR reference against wide gamut Display P3 primary color patches.

near-black-test.metaDescription: Inspect subtle dark-tone separation and shadow details near true black. Test 0% to 10% grayscale luminance steps in a darkened environment.
near-black-test.title: Near-Black & Shadow Detail Test
near-black-test.description_p1: Inspect subtle dark-tone separation and shadow transition behavior just above reference black. Low-luminance dark steps help identify black crush, elevated black floors, or panel vertical banding without claiming laboratory photometric guarantees.
instructions: VIEWING CONDITIONS: For accurate results, view this test in a dimly lit or dark room to allow your eyes to adapt to subtle dark gradations.
STEP SEPARATION: Inspect steps 0.25%, 0.5%, 1%, 2%, 3%, 4%, 5%, 6%, 8%, and 10%. Check whether the lowest steps are clearly distinct from true black (0%).
OLED & LCD DETAILS: OLED owners should check for near-black transition smoothness and vertical banding. LCD owners should inspect for elevated black floors or muddy dark detail.

gradient-banding-test.metaDescription: Test display gradient smoothness and color stepping across grayscale, RGB, and dark tonal ramps. Detect bit-depth truncation and quantization banding.
gradient-banding-test.title: Gradient & Banding Test
gradient-banding-test.description_p1: Evaluate display gradient smoothness and detect unwanted quantization banding, harsh tonal steps, or color shifts. A browser canvas cannot definitively prove panel hardware bit depth, but provides high-fidelity reference ramps for visual inspection.
instructions: GRADIENT MODES: Switch between Horizontal Grayscale, Vertical Grayscale, RGB Primaries, and Dark Shadow (0%–25%) to inspect tonal transitions across ranges.
BANDING VS SMOOTHNESS: Look for distinct vertical or horizontal stripes (stepping) across what should be continuous smooth color ramps.
QUANTIZATION COMPARISON: Toggle the 64-step quantization simulator to contrast intentional digital stepping against your display's native gradient handling.

text-clarity-test.metaDescription: Inspect text clarity, subpixel color fringing, and font rendering sharpness across multiple sizes, contrasts, and high-frequency line gratings.
text-clarity-test.title: Text Clarity & Subpixel Rendering Test
text-clarity-test.description_p1: Inspect practical on-screen text rendering clarity, edge sharpness, and subpixel color fringing. Evaluates how your display handles typography across various font sizes and contrast pairings under your current OS scaling settings.
instructions: SETUP & SCALING: Ensure browser zoom is set to 100% (Ctrl+0 / Cmd+0) and your operating system is running at native display resolution.
FONT SIZES & CONTRAST: Inspect paragraph and code samples from 8px to 32px in both positive (dark on light) and negative (light on dark) polarities.
SUBPIXEL FRINGING: Look closely at the vertical edges of black letters on white backgrounds for colored red or blue halos (common on BGR or non-standard subpixel layouts).

tv-overscan-test.metaDescription: Check if your television or external monitor is cropping desktop edges or distorting pixels. Verifies 1:1 pixel mapping and overscan settings.
tv-overscan-test.title: TV Overscan & 1:1 Pixel Mapping Test
tv-overscan-test.description_p1: Determine whether your television or external display is cropping outer desktop edges due to legacy overscan zooming. Precise 1-pixel outer borders, corner markers, and high-frequency checkerboard patterns verify true 1:1 pixel mapping.
instructions: TV PICTURE SETTINGS: On your television remote, open Picture Settings and set Aspect Ratio to 'Just Scan', 'Screen Fit', 'Dot by Dot', or '1:1' (do NOT use '16:9' or 'Zoom').
BORDER REGISTRATION: Enter Fullscreen. Check if all four outer 1px, 2px, and 5px colored border lines are fully visible around all screen edges.
CHECKERBOARD MOIRÉ: Inspect the 1:1 checkerboard patches in the center and corners. If you see wavy moiré rings or shimmering, the TV is scaling or blurring pixels.

scaling-aspect-test.metaDescription: Test display scaling uniformity and aspect ratio distortion. Features concentric true circles, square grids, and multi-aspect reference frames.
scaling-aspect-test.title: Scaling & Aspect Ratio Inspection
scaling-aspect-test.description_p1: Inspect display scaling uniformity and geometry to detect non-uniform stretching, squashing, or incorrect aspect ratio modes. Concentric circles and calibrated grid overlays expose anamorphic distortion immediately.
instructions: TRUE GEOMETRY: Inspect the concentric center circles. They must appear perfectly circular. If they look oval or egg-shaped, your display is stretching the image.
SQUARE GRID: Verify that the background grid lines form perfect equal squares rather than elongated rectangles.
ASPECT FRAMES: Switch between 16:9, 16:10, 4:3, and 21:9 reference outlines to verify how your display handles non-native content aspect ratios.

multi-touch-test.metaDescription: Test simultaneous touch screen contacts, multi-finger gesture tracking, and digitizer edge registration. Free online browser multi-touch tester.
multi-touch-test.title: Standalone Multi-Touch Test
multi-touch-test.description_p1: This test allows you to verify simultaneous touch contacts and pointer tracking on touchscreens, tablets, and multi-touch digitizers. Browser and operating system gesture engines observe and report active contacts, which may differ from physical digitizer hardware limits.
instructions: FREE TOUCH MODE: Place multiple fingers on the surface simultaneously. Observe the active contact counter, individual pointer IDs, coordinates, and peak simultaneous touch count.
MULTI-TOUCH GRID: Touch different grid cells to verify that simultaneous contacts across separate screen quadrants register accurately without phantom ghost touches.
HOLD & EDGE TARGETS: Test the simultaneous hold challenge (holding 3–5 fingers for 1.5 seconds) and touch the outer perimeter and corners to test digitizer edge rejection.

accelerometer-test.metaDescription: Test your device accelerometer and motion sensors online. Real-time 3-axis linear acceleration and gravity vector telemetry in your browser.
accelerometer-test.title: Accelerometer Test
accelerometer-test.description_p1: This test displays real-time motion and acceleration telemetry reported by your browser via DeviceMotionEvent. It observes linear acceleration and gravitational forces without claiming laboratory-grade physical sensor calibration.
instructions: START MOTION SENSOR: Click 'Start Sensor' to begin reading motion events. On iOS devices, tap 'Allow' when the browser requests permission to access motion sensors.
2D G-FORCE RETICLE: Tilt your phone or tablet in any direction. The visual reticle puck will displace according to gravitational pull along the X and Y axes.
3-AXIS TELEMETRY: Inspect linear acceleration (excluding gravity) and total acceleration (including gravity) across X, Y, and Z axes to verify sensor responsiveness.

gyroscope-test.metaDescription: Test device orientation, angular rotation, roll, pitch, and yaw angles online. Live artificial horizon attitude indicator and compass heading check.
gyroscope-test.title: Gyroscope Test
gyroscope-test.description_p1: This test exposes browser-reported angular orientation and rotational movement via DeviceOrientationEvent. Values reflect operating system calculations and do not verify physical MEMS gyroscope calibration or mechanical drift.
instructions: ENABLE GYROSCOPE: Click 'Start Sensor' to begin listening to orientation events. Confirm any browser permission prompts on mobile devices.
ATTITUDE INDICATOR: Rotate and pitch your device. The artificial horizon gauge will reflect roll (gamma) and pitch (beta) relative to the horizon plane.
EULER ANGLES: Inspect Alpha (compass yaw 0°–360°), Beta (pitch -180°–180°), and Gamma (roll -90°–90°) to evaluate smooth angular tracking.

vibration-test.metaDescription: Test your mobile phone vibration motor and haptic feedback online. Pulse presets, custom vibration sequences, and safety-limited haptic patterns.
vibration-test.title: Vibration Test
vibration-test.description_p1: Test tactile vibration motor feedback and haptic actuator response using the browser Vibration API. The browser engine can only verify that a command was accepted; physical tactile vibration must be observed and confirmed by the user.
instructions: PRESET PULSES: Tap Short (100ms), Medium (300ms), or Long (600ms) to test standard tactile feedback pulses on your mobile device.
CUSTOM SEQUENCE: Enter comma-separated pulse and pause durations in milliseconds (e.g. 200, 100, 200) to test custom rhythmic haptic sequences within safe duration limits.
OBSERVATION CHECK: Because browsers cannot measure physical motor movement, record whether you physically felt the vibration in your hand.

webcam-test.metaDescription: Test your webcam and camera stream online. Real-time video preview, browser-reported resolution and frame rate, and 100% private local snapshots.
webcam-test.title: Webcam Test

instructions: START CAMERA: Click 'Start Camera' to initiate the video stream. Confirm the browser permission dialog to allow video access (microphone access is never requested).
CAMERA SELECTION & MIRRORING: If multiple cameras are attached, select between front and rear cameras. Toggle the mirror button for natural mirror-image viewing.
TELEMETRY & LOCAL SNAPSHOT: Review browser-reported resolution and frame rate. Click 'Snapshot' to capture a private test frame in browser memory for local download.

speaker-test.metaDescription: Test your computer and monitor speakers online. Verify left and right channel separation, audio balance, test tones (100Hz–2500Hz), and frequency sweeps.
speaker-test.title: Speaker Test
speaker-test.description_p1: Verify audio output functionality, stereo channel separation, and frequency response using synthesized test tones. Digital audio waveforms test channel routing and balance, but do not measure physical acoustic distortion or room sound pressure levels.
instructions: SAFE VOLUME WARNING: Start at a low volume level and increase gradually. Avoid sustained high-volume tones through headphones or near-field monitors.
STEREO CHANNEL SEPARATION: Switch between Left Only (pan -1.0), Stereo Center, and Right Only (pan +1.0) to confirm channels are wired correctly and not reversed.
FREQUENCY TEST TONES: Test Low Bass (100 Hz), Mid Range (440 Hz concert A), High Treble (2,500 Hz), and the 4-second frequency sweep to identify speaker buzz or distortion.

microphone-test.metaDescription: Test your microphone and audio input online. Live audio level meter, waveform oscilloscope, digital clipping indicator, and local in-browser loopback check.
microphone-test.title: Microphone Test
microphone-test.description_p1: Verify microphone connectivity, browser audio capture, and relative input amplitude. Screen Tester does not upload captured microphone audio or recordings to its servers. Audio processing and recordings are handled locally in the browser.
instructions: START MICROPHONE: Click 'Start Microphone' and allow browser audio access when prompted (video is never requested).
INPUT LEVEL & WAVEFORM: Speak or make sound toward the microphone. Verify that the waveform oscillates and the live input meter registers between 30% and 80%.
LOCAL LOOPBACK & OBSERVATION: Record a 5-second sample to listen to your captured audio locally (headphones recommended to avoid acoustic feedback), then record your observation.

explain.title: WHAT DOES THIS MEAN?
explain.logicalResDesc: Also called CSS resolution, this is the grid your browser uses to render content. OS scaling and browser zoom can make this lower than your physical panel resolution.
explain.physicalResDesc: The physical pixel grid built into your display panel. Running at non-native resolutions involves scaling and can make text appear softer.
explain.dprDesc: DPR is how many physical device pixels are used to draw a single CSS pixel. A DPR of 2 means a 10x10 CSS box uses 20x20 physical pixels.
explain.ppiDesc: Pixel density (PPI) describes how many pixels are packed into each inch of the display. Higher PPI means sharper text and images, assuming the viewing distance is the same.
explain.refreshDesc: Higher resolution increases rendering workload. Higher refresh rate increases frame delivery requirements. The available combination depends on your GPU, connection bandwidth, and display.

troubleshoot.title: TROUBLESHOOTING
troubleshoot.q1: My resolution is lower than expected.
troubleshoot.a1: Check OS display scaling (e.g., 150%). This reduces the logical resolution reported to the browser. Also check browser zoom settings.
troubleshoot.a2: Check that the OS output is set to 4K. If you are mirroring a lower-resolution laptop screen, the external monitor will look blurry.
troubleshoot.a3: Check your cable. Some high resolution + high refresh combinations require DisplayPort 1.4 or HDMI 2.1. Older cables may limit you to 60Hz.

faq.title: FAQ
faq.q1: Can a browser detect my monitor's true physical resolution?
faq.a1: Not reliably. Browsers see the logical resolution and scaling factor provided by the OS. If scaling is applied, the physical resolution cannot be guaranteed.
faq.a2: This is common on Windows laptops (e.g., 125% or 150% scaling) to make text readable on high-DPI screens without making everything tiny.
faq.q3: Why is my observed frame timing different from my monitor's refresh rate?
faq.a3: Browser frame timing is affected by system load, power saving, background tabs, and browser behavior. It is an approximation, not a direct hardware query.

ghostingConcept.metaTitle: How to Check Monitor Ghosting – Pixel Response Time & Overdrive Guide
ghostingConcept.metaDescription: Learn what monitor ghosting and inverse ghosting (coronas) are, how to inspect pixel response times, and how to tune overdrive.
ghostingConcept.title: How to Check Monitor Ghosting & Motion Clarity
ghostingConcept.intro: Monitor ghosting occurs when liquid crystals take too long to transition from one color or brightness level to another. Understanding the visual symptoms helps you fine-tune your monitor's overdrive settings for optimal clarity.

standardGhosting.title: Standard Ghosting (Trailing)
standardGhosting.desc: A fuzzy, dark or smudged trail following behind moving objects against contrasting backgrounds.
standardGhosting.cause: Slow Gray-to-Gray (GtG) pixel response times. Typical on standard VA panels in dark transitions.
standardGhosting.solution: Increase the monitor's OSD Overdrive / Trace Free / AMA setting by one step.

inverseGhosting.title: Inverse Ghosting (Coronas / Overshoot)
inverseGhosting.desc: A bright, inverted-colored or glowing halo trailing behind moving objects.
inverseGhosting.cause: Excessive panel overdrive voltage pushing liquid crystals past target color states (overshoot).
inverseGhosting.solution: Lower the monitor's Overdrive setting. Never use 'Extreme' or 'Fastest' mode unless running at maximum refresh rate.

ghostingConcept.howToTestTitle: How to Test Motion Clarity in Your Browser
ghostingConcept.howToTestP1: Open our Ghosting and Motion Blur tests at full screen. Focus your gaze on a moving shape as it passes across the display. If the shape leaves a dark smear behind, overdrive is set too low. If you observe a bright, unnatural glow, overdrive is set too aggressively.
ghostingConcept.howToTestP2: Important Limitation: While browser tests provide accurate visual cues for adjusting monitor overdrive, true response times (GtG in milliseconds) require specialized high-speed photodiode oscilloscopes.
ghostingConcept.ghostingTestDesc: High contrast moving blocks across various speed profiles
ghostingConcept.refreshRateTestDesc: Measure browser frame timing and animation fluidity

backlightBleedConcept.metaTitle: How to Check Backlight Bleed vs IPS Glow – Dark Room Testing Guide
backlightBleedConcept.metaDescription: Learn how to differentiate true backlight bleed from normal IPS glow, proper dark room testing methods, and when to request an RMA.
backlightBleedConcept.title: Backlight Bleed vs IPS Glow: Testing & Diagnosis
backlightBleedConcept.intro: When viewing dark scenes on an LCD monitor, light imperfections are often noticed in corners or along the bezel edges. Differentiating structural backlight bleed from normal IPS optical glow is critical before deciding to RMA a display.

backlightBleed.title: Backlight Bleed
backlightBleed.desc: Unintended light leaking from behind the LCD matrix through uneven bezel pressure, loose frame tolerances, or pinched panel corners.
backlightBleed.behavior: Remains fixed in the exact same spot and brightness regardless of your viewing angle or viewing distance.
backlightBleed.appearance: Jagged white or yellow light puddles spilling inwards from the edges or corners.
backlightBleed.action: Severe bleed affecting daily usage justifies a retailer exchange.

ipsGlow.title: IPS Glow
ipsGlow.desc: An inherent optical phenomenon of In-Plane Switching liquid crystal panels where light reflects at wide viewing angles.
ipsGlow.behavior: Changes intensity, shifts position, or disappears entirely as you tilt your head or step further back from the screen.
ipsGlow.appearance: A soft silver, amber, or violet sheen primarily visible in the 4 corners on dark backgrounds.
ipsGlow.action: Present on almost all IPS panels; mitigated by lowering brightness and maintaining arm's-length viewing distance.

isolationSteps: Dim the room lights completely so reflections do not mask dark details.
Open our full screen Backlight Bleed test.
Set your monitor brightness to your normal working level (around 120-150 nits, usually 30-50% on monitor OSD).
Look at the corners from an arm's length. Now step back 2 meters and bob your head side to side.
If the light shifts with your head position, it is IPS glow. If the light stays anchored to the bezel edge, it is backlight bleed.

backlightBleedConcept.uniformityTestDesc: Inspect gray and luminance steps across screen quadrants

pixelDefectsConcept.metaTitle: Dead Pixel vs Stuck Pixel – How to Diagnose & Fix Screen Defects
pixelDefectsConcept.metaDescription: Understand the differences between dead pixels and stuck subpixels, how to test for them, and manufacturer warranty policies.
pixelDefectsConcept.title: Dead Pixel vs Stuck Pixel: How to Tell the Difference
pixelDefectsConcept.intro: Pixel flaws are among the most common defects found in LCD and OLED panels. Knowing whether an aberrant pixel is permanently dead or merely stuck determines whether it can be recovered or warrants a manufacturer warranty return.

deadPixel.title: Dead Pixel
deadPixel.desc: A pixel whose transistor has completely failed, leaving all three RGB subpixels permanently switched off (or unpowered).
deadPixel.appearance: Always appears pitch black against white and colored backgrounds.
deadPixel.cause: Broken electrode, failed thin-film transistor (TFT), or severed micro-trace.
deadPixel.recovery: Hardware-level failure; cannot be fixed via software cycling.

stuckPixel.title: Stuck Pixel
stuckPixel.desc: A pixel where one or two subpixels (Red, Green, or Blue) remain constantly energised and cannot turn off.
stuckPixel.appearance: A bright red, green, blue, cyan, or magenta dot, most noticeable against dark or black backgrounds.
stuckPixel.cause: Liquid crystal molecules temporarily locked in open state or charge imbalance.
stuckPixel.recovery: Rapid high-frequency color flashing (stuck pixel cycle) can sometimes unstick the crystal orientation.

pixelDefectsConcept.isoP1: Most consumer monitors are classified as Class 2 panels. Under ISO standards, manufacturers allow up to 2 permanently bright pixels, 2 permanently dark pixels, or up to 5 defective subpixels per million pixels before considering the panel defective for warranty replacement.
pixelDefectsConcept.isoP2: If you have discovered a pixel defect within the retailer's initial return or exchange window (typically 14 to 30 days), return it directly to the retailer rather than filing a manufacturer warranty claim, which may be rejected under Class 2 allowances.
pixelDefectsConcept.deadPixelTestDesc: Cycle through full screen solid white and primary colors

viewingAngles.metaDescription: Understand how monitor viewing angles affect color shift, contrast loss, and gamma changes off-axis, and how to visually inspect your display.
viewingAngles.title: Monitor Viewing Angles Explained: Color & Contrast Shift
viewingAngles.intro: Viewing angle describes how far off-axis you can view a screen before noticeable changes in brightness, contrast, or color fidelity occur. Understanding panel physics helps distinguish normal optical behavior from panel defects.
viewingAngles.keyTakeaway: Screen Tester cannot measure your monitor's physical viewing angle in degrees (e.g. 178°) through the browser. Instead, our interactive test provides controlled visual inspection patterns to evaluate color shift, gamma changes, and black-level stability.
viewingAngles.panelsSubtitle: Different liquid crystal alignments and emissive pixels create distinctly different off-axis viewing characteristics:
viewingAngles.ipsDesc: Liquid crystals rotate horizontally parallel to the glass substrate. Colors remain stable across wide horizontal and vertical angles. However, dark backgrounds exhibit 'IPS glow' (a silver or amber sheen when viewed obliquely), which is an inherent optical characteristic rather than a defect.
viewingAngles.vaDesc: Liquid crystals align vertically when unpowered, effectively blocking backlight light to achieve deep blacks (3,000:1+ contrast). Off-axis, VA panels exhibit noticeable gamma shift: dark shadow details wash out or appear lifted when viewed even slightly off-center.
viewingAngles.tnDesc: Fast response times but restrictive viewing angles. Viewing from below causes dramatic dark color inversion, while viewing from above causes severe contrast washout.
viewingAngles.oledDesc: Each pixel emits light individually without a liquid crystal shutter or backlight. Contrast remains virtually infinite at wide angles. Some OLED panels may show minor white-point tint shifts (pinkish or greenish) due to anti-glare coatings or microcavity optical layers.

effects.colorShiftDesc: Skin tones, saturated reds, or blues shifting hue or losing saturation as you move horizontally or vertically.
effects.gammaShiftDesc: Midtones and shadows becoming washed out or artificially brightened off-center (predominant on VA panels).
effects.blackLevelDesc: Deep blacks turning dark gray or developing a directional haze (IPS glow on IPS, contrast collapse on VA).

viewingAngles.howToTestTitle: How to Perform a Controlled Visual Inspection
howToTestSteps: Position yourself directly in front of the screen at your normal working distance (perpendicular normal incidence).
Launch our interactive Viewing Angle Test in fullscreen mode.
Cycle through edge-to-center targets, neutral gray fields, skin-tone swatches, and grayscale ramps.
Slowly move your head 30° to 45° to the left and right while comparing the center of the display to the corners.
Repeat vertically by viewing the display from slightly above, then from below.
Record your observations honestly: Looks normal, Slight change, Noticeable shift, or Significant shift.
viewingAngles.browserRealityTitle: What the Browser Can and Cannot Do
viewingAngles.browserCanDo: The browser can display calibrated edge-to-center targets, uniform color fields, and grayscale ramps across the entire display area to help your eyes detect off-axis variations.
viewingAngles.browserCannotDo: The browser cannot track your physical viewing position or head angle, cannot measure off-axis luminance drop in candelas, and cannot generate a hardware viewing-angle certificate.

About.missionText: Buying a new or used monitor often involves uncertainty: dead pixels, backlight bleed, washed-out contrast, and ghosting are difficult to identify during brief in-store checks or unboxings. Monitor Tester was created to provide a complete, accessible suite of diagnostic patterns that anyone can run immediately in any modern web browser.
About.howItWorksText: Every test runs locally on your device using standard HTML5 Canvas, WebGL, CSS hardware acceleration, and the Screen and Window APIs. No downloads, native installers, or administrative permissions are needed. Your display data stays entirely on your computer.
About.pixelsDesc: Detect dead pixels, stuck subpixels, bright subpixels, and panel image retention (burn-in) across pure color fields.
About.colorDesc: Evaluate continuous gradients, color banding steps, color gamut boundaries, and multi-step grayscale ramps.
About.luminanceDesc: Tune near-black and near-white clipping, check dark-room backlight bleeding, and assess full-screen brightness uniformity.
About.motionDesc: Check ghosting trails, evaluate pixel overdrive settings, measure V-Sync refresh rate (Hz), and inspect for screen tearing.
About.toolsDesc: Inspect detected screen metrics (DPR, color depth), calculate PPI and optimal viewing distances, compare displays, and test multi-touch.
About.openSourceText: Monitor Tester is an open-source project. You can inspect the source code, report rendering bugs, suggest new test patterns, or contribute directly on GitHub.

Diagnostic.noteBody: These browser tests present standard visual reference patterns to inspect pixel performance, luminance, color, and motion. They do not automatically diagnose internal component faults. If an anomaly persists across multiple browsers and devices, consult your monitor manufacturer’s warranty policy.

deadPixel.label: Dead or stuck pixel
deadPixel.desc: Tiny dark dot that won't light up, or a bright colored subpixel permanently stuck on.
deadPixel.rationale: Cycles pure primary solid color fields to visually isolate inactive black pixels from stuck red/green/blue subpixels.

strangeColors.label: Strange or washed out colors
strangeColors.desc: Tints look unnatural, dull, oversaturated, or skin tones appear tinted.
strangeColors.rationale: Evaluates standard sRGB primaries, smooth 8-bit/10-bit color ramps, and gamma tracking curves.

tooDark.label: Too dark / crushed shadows
tooDark.desc: Dark game scenes or night photos lose all detail and crush completely to black.
tooDark.rationale: Tests step-by-step luminance thresholds near 0% black so you can calibrate black level and shadow visibility.

tooBright.label: Too bright / blown-out highlights
tooBright.desc: Clouds, skies, or bright UI elements wash out and lose fine texture into pure white.
tooBright.rationale: Checks step-by-step luminance clipping from 95% to 100% white to prevent dynamic range highlight blow-out.

brightCorners.label: Bright corners / edge glow
brightCorners.desc: Corners or bezels glow brightly when displaying dark or letterboxed content.
brightCorners.rationale: Uses dark-room black fields to distinguish physical bezel pressure bleed from normal viewing-angle IPS glow.

unevenBrightness.label: Uneven brightness / dark patches
unevenBrightness.desc: Certain areas of the screen appear darker, dirty, cloudy, or vignetted.
unevenBrightness.rationale: Evaluates 5%, 15%, and 50% neutral gray fields across the entire panel to locate dirty screen effect (DSE).

blurryText.label: Blurry or fringed text
blurryText.desc: Fonts appear fuzzy, not razor-sharp, or have faint color halos along letters.
blurryText.rationale: Verifies if the OS scaling and resolution match native panel pixel layout, and inspects anti-aliasing sharpness.

motionTrails.label: Motion trails / ghosting
motionTrails.desc: Objects leave a visible blur, smudge, or trailing shadow when moving across the screen.
motionTrails.rationale: Runs variable velocity contrast blocks to visually inspect liquid crystal transition lag and overdrive tuning.

flickering.label: Screen flickering / eye strain
flickering.desc: Subtle rapid pulsing, luminance shimmering, or strain during extended viewing.
flickering.rationale: Tests high-speed alternating frame patterns to evaluate PWM backlight sensitivity and frame timing stability.

screenTearing.label: Screen tearing / split lines
screenTearing.desc: Horizontal split breaks appear across the screen during fast camera pans or video.
screenTearing.rationale: Tests high-velocity oscillating lines to evaluate browser V-Sync lock and frame synchronization behavior.

imageRetention.label: Image retention / faint ghosting
imageRetention.desc: A faint after-image of static windows, taskbars, or logos lingers on the screen.
imageRetention.rationale: Displays multiple uniform gray and primary fields with inspection grids to reveal temporary retention or burn-in.

somethingElse.rationale: Runs the complete fundamental display diagnostic sequence.

Faq.metaDescription: Clear, honest technical answers to common questions about browser display testing, dead pixel detection, color calibration, refresh rate, and resolution.
Faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
Faq.description: Honest, technical answers explaining what browser-based tests can inspect, what they cannot measure, and how to get the most accurate results.

q1.question: Can a browser detect dead pixels automatically?
q1.answer: No. A web browser has no optical sensor or camera to inspect physical hardware subpixels. Instead, Monitor Tester renders edge-to-edge, single-wavelength primary color fields (red, green, blue, black, white, magenta, cyan, yellow) allowing the human eye to immediately identify dark (dead) or permanently bright (stuck) subpixels with 100% precision.

q2.question: Does this work on laptops and TVs?
q2.answer: Yes. Monitor Tester is built entirely on standard Web APIs (Canvas, requestAnimationFrame, Fullscreen API, MatchMedia) and runs in any modern HTML5 browser on Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, Linux, Android, and iOS. When testing TVs via HDMI, ensure your TV's picture aspect ratio is set to 'Just Scan' / 1:1 and picture mode is set to 'PC' or 'Game' to avoid overscan cropping or heavy sharpening post-processing.

q3.question: Is my display data or test results collected?
q3.answer: No. Monitor Tester is an entirely client-side web utility. Zero diagnostic observations, hardware identifiers, or screen metrics are transmitted to any remote server or third-party tracking service. When you record test observations (PASS, CHECK, ISSUE), they are stored locally in your browser's private localStorage and can be purged at any time.

q4.question: Can this replace a hardware colorimeter or spectrophotometer?
q4.answer: No. A web browser cannot generate an ICC color profile or calibrate Delta-E accuracy without physical optical sensor hardware (e.g., Calibrite or Datacolor Spyder). Monitor Tester provides visual gradient test patterns, grayscale ramps, and color gamut boundaries (sRGB, Display P3) to tune contrast clipping, gamma, and color saturation by eye, but it is not a replacement for hardware sensor calibration.

q5.question: Can a browser measure display brightness (nits)?
q5.answer: No. Browsers cannot measure the physical photometric luminance (candela per square meter / nits) emitted by your screen's backlight or OLED organic emitters. The browser displays stepped 0% to 100% grayscale patches so you can adjust your monitor's hardware brightness and contrast dials until near-black (1–5%) and near-white (95–99%) steps are visibly distinct without clipping.

q6.question: Can a browser measure pixel response time (GtG / MPRT)?
q6.answer: No. Gray-to-Gray (GtG) transition speed requires specialized high-speed optical photodiode oscilloscopes or pursuit cameras. The browser measures frame presentation timing via requestAnimationFrame, but cannot determine how many milliseconds physical liquid crystals take to transition. The Ghosting Test provides variable-speed motion tracking blocks to help you visually tune your monitor's overdrive setting.

q7.question: Why is my reported resolution different from my monitor's advertised spec?
q7.answer: Modern operating systems use display scaling factors (such as 125%, 150%, or 200% on Retina/4K laptops) so that UI elements remain readable. The browser's window.screen dimensions report logical CSS pixels. Multiplying logical resolution by window.devicePixelRatio (DPR) reveals your screen's true physical native resolution. You can view both logical and physical values in our Display Information tool.

q8.question: Why is my refresh rate different from what my monitor supports?
q8.answer: If your 144Hz or 240Hz monitor is only reporting 60Hz in the test, common causes include: (1) Windows/macOS display settings default to 60Hz until manually set to high refresh rate in Advanced Display Settings; (2) HDMI cable bandwidth limitations (DisplayPort or HDMI 2.1 is required for high refresh at 1440p/4K); (3) Browser hardware acceleration is disabled; or (4) Battery power-saving mode is capping frame rate.
